faqs.question: Can I decorate a fire-rated office door for Halloween?
faqs.answer: Usually only lightly. The University of Missouri–Kansas City, for example, allows one sheet of paper no larger than 8.5 × 11 inches on a fire-rated door and nothing else combustible. Look for a certification label on the door's hinge edge, and ask facilities if you are unsure.

faqs.question: How much of an office door can Halloween decorations cover?
faqs.answer: It depends on your building's rule. UMKC allows up to 50% of a non-fire-rated door in a sprinklered building and 20% in an unsprinklered one, while Clarkson University caps paper at 10% of any wall or door. Ask your fire marshal or facilities team for the figure that applies to you.

faqs.question: Why can't decorations go on the hallway side of some office doors?
faqs.answer: Some policies treat the side facing the exit route as off limits. UMKC bans decorations on the egress side of any door, typically the hallway face of a door that swings outward, so it stays fully visible during an evacuation. In that case, decorate the inside face instead.

faqs.question: Can I put string lights on my office door?
faqs.answer: Check first, because many workplaces restrict them. Clarkson University bans extension cords and stringing lights over doorways, and allows no more than 3 strands joined together. A paper design with no power is the simpler choice for a door.

faqs.question: Is it OK to cover the room number sign with decorations?
faqs.answer: No. Under the 2010 ADA Standards, tactile room signs sit 48 to 60 inches above the floor on the latch side of the door, with an 18 × 18 inch clear floor space in front. Keep decorations, tape and floor props away from that sign and its braille.

faqs.question: What tape should I use to stick decorations on an office door?
faqs.answer: Use a non-damaging, removable adhesive. UMKC's guidelines ask for adhesives that do not compromise the door's surface or its fire rating, and require decorations to be securely attached so nothing hangs loose or snags.

faqs.question: How do you judge an office door decorating contest fairly?
faqs.answer: Run a safety check before judging, so any door that breaks the coverage, sign or exit rules is out first. Then score out of 20 (8 for originality, 6 for the best office in-joke, 6 for reused materials) and add a colleague vote by phone.

faqs.question: What if a coworker doesn't want their door decorated?
faqs.answer: Leave it bare and say nothing more about it. A 2026 study of 261 Hungarian physicians found one profile of staff with low engagement in workplace self-expression, so not wanting to decorate is normal, not a lack of team spirit.

faqs.question: What door ideas work for colleagues who don't celebrate Halloween?
faqs.answer: An autumn harvest door with leaves, apples and a thank-you line uses no Halloween imagery at all. Count it as a full contest entry rather than a consolation prize, and keep every theme away from mocking any faith or culture.

faqs.question: When should office Halloween door decorations come down?
faqs.answer: Soon after the day. UMKC requires decorations to come down within 30 days, and keeping temporary signs up for 7 days or less keeps them inside the ADA Standards' temporary-sign exception. Taking everything down by 1 November is a simple rule.

article.contentMarkdown:
# Halloween Door Decorating Ideas for Office: 14 Fire-Safe Builds

The safest Halloween door decorating ideas for an office are flat, paper-based designs that cover no more than half the door, keep the room sign and handle clear, and stay off fire-rated doors except for one letter-size sheet. Below are 14 original designs with build time and estimated cost, plus a five-day contest format.

Set the build window early. On SubhSandesh, 49.4% of Raksha Bandhan 2026 pages were built on the festival day itself, and 86.1% of the on-time ones within 24 hours of it; we cite that festival, a sample of 89 pages, only because no Halloween figure exists yet. Run the contest vote by phone link too, because 48.3% of shared SubhSandesh pages are opened on a phone.

## What makes an office door different from a front door?

An office door is part of a building's fire and wayfinding system, not a private surface. It may be fire-rated, it carries a room sign people navigate by, and its corridor side sits on the route everyone uses to leave in an emergency.

So the decoration has to be thin, flame-resistant and quick to remove. Halloween is Saturday 31 October 2026 and Sunday 31 October 2027, so most offices judge on the Friday before.

## The fire rules that bind an office door: 50%, 20% or one sheet

There is no single number: your fire marshal or facilities team sets it, so ask before buying supplies. Two published campus policies show how far answers differ.

The [University of Missouri–Kansas City door decoration guidelines (September 2025)](https://www.umkc.edu/insider/_files/docs/door-decoration-guildelines.pdf), written to comply with the NFPA 80 fire-door standard, set these limits for its own buildings. Treat them as an example, not your rule:

- Fire-rated doors: one sheet of paper no larger than 8.5 × 11 inches, nothing else combustible.
- Non-fire-rated office doors: up to 50% of the surface in a sprinklered building, 20% in an unsprinklered one.
- Materials flame-resistant or treated to NFPA 701, firmly attached, removed within 30 days.
- Nothing on the egress side of a door (the hallway side of an outward-swinging door), or near exit signs, extinguishers, pull stations or sprinklers.

That egress rule means many hallway-facing doors on that campus cannot be decorated at all, so the contest moves to the inside face. [Clarkson University's office and door decorating rules](https://announcements.clarkson.edu/wp-content/uploads/Office-and-Door-Decorating-Fire-Safety-Rules.pdf) cap paper at 10% of any wall or door, and ban extension cords, natural greenery and open flames.

To spot a fire-rated door, look for a certification label on its hinge edge. If it has one, choose design 1 below and stop.

## Signs, vision panels and accessibility: the 48–60 inch zone

Never cover the room sign. Under the [2010 ADA Standards, section 703](https://www.access-board.gov/ada/#ada-703), tactile room signs sit with their characters between 48 and 60 inches above the floor, alongside the door on the latch side, with an 18 × 18 inch clear floor space in front for anyone reading the braille. Three rules follow:

- Leave a margin around the room sign and never tape over its braille.
- Keep floor props out of the 18-inch square in front of the sign.
- Keep any glass vision panel clear, so people can see someone approaching.

Section 216.1 exempts temporary signs that stay up 7 days or less. Contest labels up for one week fall inside that.

## 14 office door designs with build time and cost (EST)

Every design is flat card and paper, under 50% of a standard door. Costs are estimates at US craft-store prices, October 2026, assuming flame-retardant paper.

### 1. The out-of-office ghost

One letter-size sheet laid out as an auto-reply: "I am currently haunting the third floor and will reply after 1 November." Materials: a printed sheet, removable tape. Build time 20 minutes; cost under $2 (EST). The only design here for a fire-rated door.

### 2. The retired-projects graveyard

Grey card headstones, each carrying a retired project, system or file format with its dates. Materials: grey card, marker, green paper grass. Build time 60 minutes; cost about $6 (EST).

### 3. The coffin calendar

October as a coffin-shaped month grid with the 31st circled and the 2026 and 2027 dates listed. Materials: black card, white pen, orange stickers. Build time 45 minutes; cost about $5 (EST).

### 4. The web of acronyms

A white-on-black paper web with the team's most confusing acronyms caught in it, spelled out underneath. Materials: black poster board, paint pen, a paper spider. Build time 50 minutes; cost about $7 (EST).

### 5. The sticky-note pixel pumpkin

A 12 × 12 grid of orange, black and green sticky notes forming a pumpkin, with gaps for colleagues to fill one note each. Materials: three sticky-note pads. Build time 40 minutes; cost about $8 (EST).

### 6. The posture skeleton

A paper skeleton at a desk showing correct screen height, captioned "Bad posture will haunt you." Materials: printed skeleton, card desk, split pins. Build time 60 minutes; cost about $6 (EST).

### 7. Wanted: the stapler phantom

A Wild West wanted poster for the ghost who keeps taking the stapler, reward one biscuit. Materials: kraft paper, brown marker, a printed silhouette. Build time 30 minutes; cost about $3 (EST).

### 8. The haunted inbox

A giant paper envelope with a skeleton hand reaching out and an unread counter stuck at 13. Materials: white card, printed hand, red number. Build time 35 minutes; cost about $4 (EST).

### 9. The werewolf shift rota

A weekly rota where each shift is marked by a paper moon, filling from crescent to full on Friday. Materials: grey and yellow card, marker. Build time 50 minutes; cost about $5 (EST).

### 10. The black-cat ticket queue

A queue of black paper cats holding ticket numbers, the last one asleep on the counter. Materials: black card, white pen, printed numbers. Build time 45 minutes; cost about $5 (EST).

### 11. The bookshelf of dread

Paper book spines titled "The Quarterly Report That Would Not Die" and "Return of the Reply-All". Materials: coloured card strips, gold pen. Build time 70 minutes; cost about $7 (EST).

### 12. The password crypt

A grey card crypt sealed with a paper padlock: "Some secrets stay buried: never share your password." Materials: grey card, marker, printed padlock. Build time 40 minutes; cost about $5 (EST).

### 13. The coffee cauldron menu

A paper cauldron listing the kitchen's drinks as potions, each with its real allergen note. Materials: black card, white pen, printed labels. Build time 45 minutes; cost about $5 (EST).

### 14. The harvest door

Autumn leaves, apples and a "thank you for this year" line, with no Halloween imagery. Materials: red, gold and brown card. Build time 40 minutes; cost about $5 (EST). The choice for anyone who would rather not mark Halloween.

## The 14 designs compared by coverage, time and cost

The table groups designs by how much door they use.

| Group | Designs | Door coverage | Build time | Cost (EST, Oct 2026) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| One sheet | 1 | One 8.5 × 11 in sheet | 20 min | Under $2 |
| Small panel | 7, 8, 12 | About 10–20% | 30–40 min | $3–5 |
| Half-door scene | 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 11, 13, 14 | 20–50% | 40–70 min | $5–7 |
| Group-built | 5, 10 | 20–50%, growing | 40–45 min plus additions | $5–8 |

Only design 1 suits a fire-rated door, and under a 10% paper limit only the one-sheet group and a trimmed small panel pass.

## Running a door-decorating contest: a 5-day format

Keep the contest inside one working week, under the 7-day temporary-sign line. Book the safety walk-round with facilities first.

1. Monday: announce the rules and the fire marshal's limits (26 October 2026; 25 October 2027).
2. Tuesday: teams register a door, and facilities confirms it is not fire-rated.
3. Wednesday and Thursday: build inside a two-hour window each day, so desks stay staffed.
4. Friday morning: a safety walk-round; any door failing the coverage, sign or exit check is out before judging.
5. Friday afternoon: judging and a phone vote (30 October 2026; 29 October 2027), with everything down by 1 November.

Score out of 20: 8 for originality, 6 for the best office in-joke, 6 for reused materials. Four awards spread the credit:

- The One Sheet Wonder, for the best single-sheet design.
- The Marshal's Pick, chosen by whoever ran the walk-round.
- The Second Life Award, for the most reused material.
- The Corridor Vote, decided by colleagues on their phones.

## Inclusive themes: why some colleagues will opt out

Decorating should be opt-in, door by door, because a door is personal territory. A [2026 discrete choice study of 433 university support staff](https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC12957959) found a dedicated desk mattered most to them, followed by personalisation and territoriality: the same workspace and the option to leave personal items.

A [2026 survey of 261 Hungarian physicians](https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC13088593) found three profiles of workplace self-expression, one with low engagement in it. So never decorate a colleague's door without asking, and accept "no" without comment.

In Britain, [Acas guidance says religion or belief harassment](https://www.acas.org.uk/religion-or-belief-discrimination/types-of-religion-or-belief-discrimination) can count even when it is not aimed at anyone in particular, and not having a religion is protected too. Keep themes away from mocking any faith, culture, body or real colleague, and treat design 14 as a full entry.

## Where SubhSandesh fits, and when it is the wrong tool

SubhSandesh cannot decorate a door, judge a contest or invite a team. Each Halloween page greets one person, in partner, best friend, family or kids mode, so it suits the colleague who helped build your graveyard, not the floor.

Our [five-minute interactive Halloween card](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-halloween) holds a letter, up to six photos and a pumpkin they carve with your chosen word. The [ten-minute cinematic Halloween surprise](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-halloween-premium) adds a 60-second voice note, up to 12 photos and one emailed reply. If that colleague skips Halloween, [browse every SubhSandesh template](https://subhsandesh.in/templates) for a thank-you instead.

Anything the whole office should see belongs on paper, not in a private link. A door and a handwritten note do that job better.

## Sources

- University of Missouri–Kansas City, Door Decoration Guidelines, September 2025.
- Clarkson University, Office and Door Decorating Fire Safety Rules (undated).
- U.S. Access Board, 2010 ADA Standards for Accessible Design, sections 216 and 703.
- Aboagye et al., Scandinavian Journal of Work, Environment & Health, 2026.
- Gyöngyösi et al., BMC Health Services Research, 2026.
- Acas, Types of religion or belief discrimination (undated).
